rules.classification: Spectroscopic classes and alert or messenger labels are different definitions and are not compared; two active classes differ when neither label refines the other (for example 'SN Ia' and 'SN Ia-91T' agree); an earlier value from the same provider is a revision.
rules.host: Two proposed hosts agree when their names match after case and spacing are ignored or one name is among the other's NED cross-identifications; otherwise they are an identity ambiguity. Association probabilities are not computed.
rules.photometry: Only exactly compatible photometry (same epoch, band, system, method, calibration and direct/difference state, two or more providers) is compared. The limiting magnitude or flux that a provider reports alongside a detection is that epoch's detection threshold, not a non-detection, and is not compared with the detection; a detection brighter than another provider's non-detection limit at the same epoch is a status conflict. A group is listed only when it is still inconsistent under these rules; at most 10 groups per event, most significant first.
rules.position: Two positions with no stated uncertainty are inconsistent when they are more than 2 arcsec apart; when one states an error radius, the separation is compared with 3 times that radius.
rules.redshift: Two redshifts with no stated uncertainty are inconsistent when they differ by more than 0.005 (about 1,500 km/s); transient and host redshifts are different definitions and are listed, not compared; host redshifts of differently named hosts are an identity ambiguity.
rules.revision: A retracted row, or a superseded row of the same provider whose value differs beyond the property's rule, is a revision or retraction; a revision within the rule is consistent; the earlier value stays visible.
rules.sigma: Two values that both state an uncertainty are inconsistent when they differ by more than 3 combined standard deviations (uncertainties added in quadrature; a stated position error radius is treated as one standard deviation).

W.F. Wen (SZTU), Q.H. Lao (NAO, CAS), L.N. Xu (USTC), H.Y. Liu (NAO, CAS), X.H. Tang (THU), and C.C. Jin (NAO, CAS) report on behalf of the Einstein Probe (EP) team:
We report on a further observation of the EP261007b field with the Follow-up X-ray Telescope (FXT) on board the Einstein Probe (EP) mission. The observation began at 2026-10-18T18:39:14 UTC, with an exposure of approximately 2978s.
EP261007b was initially detected by EP-WXT (Wen et al., GCN 45847), with subsequent X-ray analysis reported by Wen et al. (GCN 45872). An optical transient within the WXT localization, but outside the original FXT error circle, was reported by Quirola-Vasquez et al. (GCN 45864) and Li et al. (GCN 45870). Our FXT observation on 2026-10-10 revealed a possible X-ray counterpart located 12.6 arcsec from this optical transient (Wen et al., GCN 45902). However, this X-ray counterpart was not detected in the latest FXT observation. We derived a 3 sigma upper limit on the 0.5–10 keV flux of 9.64E-14 erg cm^-2 s^-1.
Launched on January 9, 2024, EP is a space-based X-ray observatory designed to monitor the soft X-ray sky and perform X-ray follow-up observations (Yuan et al. 2022, Handbook of X-ray and Gamma-ray Astrophysics).

W.F. Wen (SZTU), Q.H. Lao (NAO, CAS), L.N. Xu (USTC), H.Y. Liu (NAO, CAS), X.H. Tang (THU), and C.C. Jin (NAO, CAS) report on behalf of the Einstein Probe (EP) team:
The X-ray transient EP261007b was detected by the Wide-field X-ray Telescope (WXT) on board the Einstein Probe (EP) mission on 2026-10-07 (Wen et al., GCN 45847). A refined analysis of the EP-WXT and autonomous EP-FXT observations was subsequently reported by Wen et al. (GCN 45872).  Optical and near-infrared follow-up observations were reported by Ma et al. (GCN 45849), Zhang et al. (GCN 45860), Mohan et al. (GCN 45861), Shi et al. (GCN 45862), Quirola-Vasquez et al. (GCN 45864), and Li et al. (GCN 45870).
The EP-FXT performed a second follow-up observation of EP261007b beginning at 2026-10-10T04:43:36 (UTC), with an exposure of about 3566 s. No significant X-ray source was detected at the position of EP261007b. We derived a 3σ upper limit on its 0.5–10 keV flux of 2.3 × 10^-13 erg cm^-2 s^-1. This result indicates that the X-ray emission had faded since the initial EP observation.
Quirola-Vasquez et al. (GCN 45864) reported an optical transient outside the original FXT error circle. The transient was subsequently confirmed in archival SVOM/VT observations by Li et al. (GCN 45870). In the second FXT observation, an X-ray source was detected at R.A. = 356.3435 deg, Decl. = 11.3440 deg (J2000), with an offset of 12.6 arcsec from the optical position. The 0.5–10 keV spectrum from FXT-B is reasonably well fitted by an absorbed power-law model with the hydrogen column density fixed at the Galactic value. The best-fit photon index is 3.1 (+2.5/-2.2), corresponding to an unabsorbed 0.5–10 keV flux of 6.27 × 10^-14 erg cm^-2 s^-1.
Given its close proximity, this X-ray source might be associated with the optical source reported in GCN 45864 and GCN 45870, although additional observations are needed to firmly establish the connection.
We encourage further multiwavelength observations of EP261007b and the possible X-ray counterpart to the optical transient.
Launched on January 9, 2024, EP is a space-based X-ray observatory designed to monitor the soft X-ray sky and perform X-ray follow-up observations (Yuan et al. 2022, Handbook of X-ray and Gamma-ray Astrophysics).

We report on a further observation of the EP261007b field with the Follow-up X-ray Telescope (FXT) on board the Einstein Probe (EP) mission. The observation began at 2026-10-18T18:39:14 UTC, with an exposure of approximately 2978s.
EP261007b was initially detected by EP-WXT (Wen et al., GCN 45847), with subsequent X-ray analysis reported by Wen et al. (GCN 45872). An optical transient within the WXT localization, but outside the original FXT error circle, was reported by Quirola-Vasquez et al. (GCN 45864) and Li et al. (GCN 45870). Our FXT observation on 2026-10-10 revealed a possible X-ray counterpart located 12.6 arcsec from this optical transient (Wen et al., GCN 45902). However, this X-ray counterpart was not detected in the latest FXT observation. We derived a 3 sigma upper limit on the 0.5–10 keV flux of 9.64E-14 erg cm^-2 s^-1.
Launched on January 9, 2024, EP is a space-based X-ray observatory designed to monitor the soft X-ray sky and perform X-ray follow-up observations (Yuan et al. 2022, Handbook of X-ray and Gamma-ray Astrophysics).
